[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hafuri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja {{Infobox religious building | name = Niutsuhime Jinja
丹生都比売神社 | image = Niutsuhime-jinja dai2-3honden.jpg | caption = Honden of Niutsuhime Jinja | map_type = Japan Wakayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|15|45.80|N|135|31|10.20|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Niutsuhime Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami]]
[[Kōyamiko-no-Ōkami]]
[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hafuri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja {{Infobox religious building | name = Niutsuhime Jinja
丹生都比売神社 | image = Niutsuhime-jinja dai2-3honden.jpg | caption = Honden of Niutsuhime Jinja | map_type = Japan Wakayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|15|45.80|N|135|31|10.20|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Niutsuhime Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami]]
[[Kōyamiko-no-Ōkami]]
[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hafuri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja {{Infobox religious building | name = Niutsuhime Jinja
丹生都比売神社 | image = Niutsuhime-jinja dai2-3honden.jpg | caption = Honden of Niutsuhime Jinja | map_type = Japan Wakayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|15|45.80|N|135|31|10.20|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Niutsuhime Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami]]
[[Kōyamiko-no-Ōkami]]
[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja {{Infobox religious building | name = Niutsuhime Jinja
丹生都比売神社 | image = Niutsuhime-jinja dai2-3honden.jpg | caption = Honden of Niutsuhime Jinja | map_type = Japan Wakayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|15|45.80|N|135|31|10.20|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Niutsuhime Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami]]
[[Kōyamiko-no-Ōkami]]
[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja {{Infobox religious building | name = Niutsuhime Jinja
丹生都比売神社 | image = Niutsuhime-jinja dai2-3honden.jpg | caption = Honden of Niutsuhime Jinja | map_type = Japan Wakayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|15|45.80|N|135|31|10.20|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Niutsuhime Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami]]
[[Kōyamiko-no-Ōkami]]
[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja [[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja [[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja [[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja {{Infobox religious building | name = Niutsuhime Jinja
丹生都比売神社 | image = Niutsuhime-jinja dai2-3honden.jpg | caption = Honden of Niutsuhime Jinja | map_type = Japan Wakayama Prefecture#Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|34|15|45.80|N|135|31|10.20|E|type:landmark_region:JP|display=title, inline}} | map_relief = 1 | map_size = | map_caption = Niutsuhime Jinja | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = | deity = [[Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami]]
[[Kōyamiko-no-Ōkami]]
[[Ōgetsuhime-no-kami]]
[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]] | founded_by = | established = Unknown, before 9th century | date_destroyed = | location = 230 Kami-amano, Katsuragi-chō, Ito-gun, Wakayama-ken 649-7141 | website = {{Official|1=http://www.niutsuhime.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' | festival = October 16 | leadership = | designation1 = World Heritage Site | designation1_type = Cultural | designation1_criteria = ii, iv | designation1_date = 2004 | designation1_number = [https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1142bis] | footnotes = {{box|background=white|align=center|wide=yes|border size=3px|border color=brown|text align=center|[[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site of Japan]]}} }} The {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime Shrine''' or '''Nibutsuhime Shrine'''|丹生都比売神社|Niutsuhime-jinja, Nibutsuhime-jinja|}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in located the town of [[Katsuragi, Wakayama|Katsuragi]], [[Ito District, Wakayama|Ito district]], [[Wakayama Prefecture]], [[Japan]]. The shrine is one of three shrines claiming the title of ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]]. Also known as "Amano Taisha" and "Amano Shisho Myojin", it is the head shrine of about 180 Niutsuhime Shrines around the country. Its precincts are designated a [[Monuments of Japan|National Historic Site]]{{cite web|url=https://bunka.nii.ac.jp/heritages/detail/173885|title=丹生都比売神社境内 |work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2020}} and the shrine is one of the constituent assets of the [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] ''[[Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range]]''. ==Overview== The shrine is located in the Amano basin, northwest of [[Mount Koya]] in the northeastern part of Wakayama prefecture. The [[Kōyasan chōishi-michi]], the path to Mount Koya lined with stone markers (itself a National Historic Site and World Heritage Site) passes on the ridge of the hill behind the shrine. The ''[[kasuga-zukuri]]'' style [[Honden]] and the [[Rōmon]] gate of the shrine are both National [[Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Important Cultural Properties]].{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2869|title=丹生都比売神社楼門|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}}{{cite web|url=https://kunishitei.bunka.go.jp/heritage/detail/102/2870|title=丹生都比売神社本殿|work=Cultural Heritage Online|publisher=Agency for Cultural Affairs|language=Japanese|accessdate=5 April 2021}} There are four ''kami'' worshipped at Niutsuhime Shrine: * {{nihongo|'''Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami'''|丹生都比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Niutsu-myōjin'''|丹生明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''Takanomiko-no-Ōkami'''|高野御子大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kariba-myōjin'''|狩場明神||}} * {{nihongo|'''[[Ukemochi |Ōgetsuhime-no-Ōkami]]'''|大食津比売大神||}}, also known as {{nihongo|'''Kihi-myōjin'''|気比明神||}} (brought from [[Kehi Shrine]] in 1208 * {{nihongo|'''[[Benzaiten |Ichikishimahime-no-Ōkami]]'''|市杵島比売大神||}}, brought from [[Itsukushima Shrine]] in 1208 ==History== The foundation of Niutsuhime Shrine is uncertain. Per the "Harima Kokudo Fudoki", a ''[[kami]]'' named "Niutsuhime no Mikoto" , and this has been equated with Niutsuhime Shrine. The "Harima Kokudo Fudoki" goes on to describe how [[Empress Jingu]] consulted the oracle of this shrine prior to her conquest of Korea, and the ''[[Nihon Shoki]]'' names the local ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' as "Amano-no-Hōri" and states that he donated red clay ([[cinnabar]]) as a token of victory. The enshrined ''kami'', Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami, is the younger sister of [[Amaterasu]] an is credited with land clearing in parts of [[Yamato province]] and the [[Kii Peninsula]] to bring agriculture to the land. The location of the shrine was given as the eastern peak of Kamitsutsuga, near the water source of the Nyukawa River. This area is still regarded as the former enshrined place of Niutsuhime Shrine, which was relocated to its current site due to the construction of [[Kongōbu-ji]] in the early [[Heian period]]. In the ''[[Konjaku Monogatari]]'',Takanomiko-no-Ōkami, the son of Niutsuhime-no-Ōkami assumed the form of a hunter with two black and white dogs, and led [[Kūkai]] into the mountains, where he later built [[Mount Koya]] on what was formerly the site of the shrine. The shrine was rebuilt a short distance away to be the guardian shrine of the temple. By the end of the 10th century, the shine was officially regarded as being a part of the temple. The shrine is mentioned in the 927 AD ''[[Engishiki]]'' records as receiving an annual stipend from the Court. Due to its strong connection with Mount Koya, branches of the shrine were established in many locations in conjunction with the spread of [[Shingon Buddhism]]. During the [[Kamakura period]], the oracle of the shrine predicted the [[Mongol invasions of Japan]], and the shrine took the lead in prayers for divine intervention which led to the Japanese victory. It came to be described in contemporary literature as the ''[[ichinomiya]]'' of [[Kii Province]], although there are several other shrines within Kii Province with an older claim to that title. It was the custom for pilgrims to Mount Koya to pay a visit to this shrine before visiting the temple. The shrine became independent of Mount Koya following the [[Meiji restoration]], although many Buddhist relics remain within its precincts due to its long association with Mount Koya. The shrine was designated a prefectural shrine in 1873 under the [[Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines]] within [[State Shinto]]. It was promoted to an {{nihongo|Imperial shrines, 1st rank|官幣大社|kanpei taisha}} in 1924. It still retains close ties with Mount Koya, and monks reciting Buddhist sutras in front of the shrine is a common sight. ==Gallery== Niutsuhime-jinja roumon.JPG| Rōmon, National ICP Niutsuhimejinja 05.JPG|Honden,National ICP ==See also== *[[List of National Treasures of Japan (crafts-swords)]] *[[List of Historic Sites of Japan (Wakayama)]] ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category|Niutsuhime-jinja}} *[https://niutsuhime.or.jp/en// Official Home Page] {{Shinto shrine}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{draft categories| [[Category:11]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category:Pages that used to use Authority control]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:beppyo shrines without templates]] [[Category:Kanpei Taisha]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Wakayama Prefecture]] [[Category:Katsuragi, Wakayama]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Historic Sites of Japan]] [[Category:Myōjin Taisha]] [[Category:Kōyasan]] [[Category:Wakayama Prefecture designated tangible cultural property]] [[Category:Kasuga-zukuri]] [[Category:1 revision imported]] [[Category:New]] [[Category:C111]] [[Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia]] }} [[en:Niutsuhime Shrine]] [[sn:Niutsuhime Shrine]] [[ja:%E4%B8%B9%E7%94%9F%E9%83%BD%E6%AF%94%E5%A3%B2%E7%A5%9E%E7%A4%BE]]
